questions.title: Two behaviours disagree about region:CompletionGrid.days

sides.title: The history window is whatever the caller asks for

questions.asks: The two sides only contradict each other on paper — the route is caller-supplied DEFAULTING to 30, which satisfies both. The real collision underneath is the NAME: DESIGN.md documents ?days=30, the route binds ?historyDays. Which one is the contract the frontend gets built against?

options.label: Rename the code to days
options.consequence: HabitRoutes.cs:68 binds `int days = 30` and HabitApiTests.cs:182 follows. A frontend written from DESIGN.md then works. It is a breaking query-parameter change to a route, and the generated API client needs regenerating.

options.label: Rename the design to historyDays
options.consequence: DESIGN.md:83 becomes ?historyDays=30. No code moves, no client regenerates, nothing can break. The document a human and an assistant read to build the screen gets the uglier of the two names.

recommend.label: Rename the code to days
recommend.why: This is the cheapest it will ever be: the history screen is habits#13, unbuilt, so there is no consumer to break today and exactly one after it lands. And your own frontend-first rule points this way — the parameter is named by what the screen asks for, not by a handler's local variable. The response body already returns a `days` array, so ?days=7 returning seven days reads as one idea rather than two.

questions.against: Nothing is actually broken right now: the default is 30 either way, so the only caller that gets hurt is one written from the doc that also passes the parameter, and none exists. Editing one line of prose is a strictly smaller change than editing a route, a test and a regenerated client, and it carries no chance of breaking a deploy. `historyDays` is also the more explicit name at the call site — `?days` sitting next to a `days` array in the response can read as though it filters that field rather than sizing it. And 'rename it now while it is free' is the argument that gets made immediately before the first consumer appears.

options.label: Add the view
options.consequence: DESIGN.md MVP 4 gains an archived view. The flag earns a documented reason to exist and the frontend gets something to build. More surface on an app whose screens are not built yet.

options.label: Delete the flag
options.consequence: GetAll stops taking it and one backend test goes with it. Archived habits stay retrievable by id (BEH-ARCHIVE-1), so nothing is lost — but un-archiving through the UI becomes a new decision if you ever want it.

recommend.label: Add the view
recommend.why: Archiving is already a one-way door in the UI: DELETE archives rather than deletes, so a habit archived by mistake is reachable from no documented screen. The flag is not spare surface — it is the missing half of a capability MVP 4 already promises.

questions.against: MVP 4 promises archiving, not un-archiving, and none of the three screens exists yet — this adds scope to an app whose Today screen is not built. Deleting the flag costs one test, and the day you want the view you write it then against a design that states it. Keeping unused surface because it might be needed is exactly how an API grows features nobody asked for.

questions.asks: Nothing documented displays an error. Should DESIGN.md gain an error state the frontend renders these into, or should the machine-readable code go and a status code be the whole contract?

options.label: Document the error state
options.consequence: DESIGN.md gains a row saying what each screen shows when a habit 404s and when the API 500s. The error code earns a purpose — the frontend maps code to copy. Costs a design edit now, and commits three screens that do not exist yet to per-code messages.

options.label: Drop the code, keep the status
options.consequence: ProblemDetails stays, the bespoke code goes, and one backend test simplifies. The frontend shows one generic failure. You lose the ability to tell 'this habit was archived' apart from 'that id was never real' without adding the code back later.

recommend.label: Document the error state
recommend.why: A 404 here is not an exotic path — it is a direct consequence of A5. DELETE archives rather than deletes, so any list the client is holding can name an id the backend now refuses. Undocumented means the frontend author invents the behaviour at the keyboard, which is the thing this corpus exists to stop.

questions.against: A6 says single user, and a single user on a single device reaches that stale-id race close to never — so the case above is largely hypothetical, and it is being used to add scope to an app whose Today screen is not built. There is also a cheaper middle this question does not offer: document ONE generic error state, leave the code in the payload unconsumed, and decide per-code copy on the day a second code actually distinguishes something. Picking the full version now spends design effort on branches that may never be rendered.

questions.title: Edits are held until Commit, so a half-described change never reaches a branch
questions.asks: Does a hosted edit write to GitHub immediately, or accumulate until Commit?

options.label: Accumulate until Commit
options.consequence: the Commit button is the only thing that talks to GitHub; a change spanning three behaviours lands as one commit, and abandoning it costs nothing

options.label: Write each edit straight through
options.consequence: no server-side state at all, and the pod can die mid-change without losing anything; but every keystroke-level save is a commit, and a spec described over five edits arrives as five red branches

recommend.label: Accumulate until Commit
recommend.why: your own sentence puts Commit at the end of a list of edits — 'add new behaviours, update behaviours, remove behaviours etc and then can Commit' — which reads as a staging step. And a change is usually more than one behaviour: BEH-PULL-2 and BEH-PULL-3 above are one decision of yours described twice.

questions.against: Accumulating means the pod holds unsaved work, and you said there is no volume for it — a restart between your last edit and Commit loses the lot. Writing straight through cannot lose anything, and five small PRs are annoying rather than dangerous.

questions.title: Every pool operation is scoped to one language
contracts: bootstrap for one language leaves another language's pool untouched
the loader throws when the language is missing
questions.asks: DESIGN.md defers other languages but promises the data model is language-tagged from day one. It got more than a column: `language` is a required parameter on all three IPoolService methods, so every drill route in PR 4 has to carry it too. Is language a PARAMETER, or a setting the app is configured with?

options.label: Keep it threaded
options.consequence: IPoolService.cs:17,24,31 keep `string language`, and the drill routes take it as a path segment or query param. The isolation property stays enforced. Adding Cantonese is then a seed file and a config value, with no signature to change and no migration. Cost: every route, client call and test in PR 4 carries an argument whose only possible value today is `zh`.

options.label: Make it ambient
options.consequence: Drop the parameter; one configured language, resolved from settings or an owner record. VocabItemEntity.cs:14 already defaults Language to \"zh\", so the column and the seed loader's per-language files survive untouched — the roadmap promise DESIGN.md actually makes is kept. The isolation test loses its subject, and language 2 becomes a signature change across the service, the routes and the client.

recommend.label: Keep it threaded
recommend.why: The parameter is not speculative surface — it is the roadmap promise DESIGN.md:36-37 states, made executable. And the moment to pay for it is now, before PR 4 exists: threading it through routes that are not written yet costs one argument each, where retrofitting it later means changing a shipped API and regenerating a client. A6-style single-user apps are also where an ambient global is hardest to unpick, because the assumption gets read into a dozen call sites first.

questions.against: The isolation test seeds a synthetic \"fr\" that exists nowhere else in the repo — 150 HSK1 entries in one file, one language, zero users asking for a second. So a required argument is being carried on every method and every future route to satisfy a property no caller can exercise, and the test proves the code does what it was written to do rather than anything about the product. \"Other languages\" is under **Explicitly deferred**, and a deferred feature that still shapes today's signatures has not really been deferred. The cheap version is to keep the Language COLUMN — which is all DESIGN.md literally promises — and let the parameter arrive with the second language, when its shape will be known rather than guessed.

questions.title: A vocabulary item has a type, defaulting to word
contracts: the schema reserves a Sentence type that nothing produces or consumes
questions.asks: The string `Sentence` occurs exactly twice in this repo: the enum member, and the DESIGN.md line reserving it. No seed entry sets a type, no route exposes one, the frontend has no such field. Does the reservation stay, or does the type arrive with sentence mode?

options.label: Keep the reservation
options.consequence: VocabItemType.cs keeps `Sentence = 1`. It pins `Word = 0` as the default, so the enum can be extended later without renumbering a persisted column, and it makes DESIGN.md:34-35's second phase legible in the code a reader actually opens.

options.label: Drop it until it is built
options.consequence: The enum becomes `Word = 0` alone. Adding a member back later is one line and no migration, since nothing has ever persisted a 1. The type column, the nullable SeedEntry.Type and the defaulting test all survive — only the unreachable value goes.

recommend.label: Keep the reservation
recommend.why: This is the cheapest kind of reserved surface there is: an enum member costs no route, no client field, no migration and no test, and it is the one place a persisted integer genuinely benefits from being fixed early — `Word = 0` is only guaranteed if nothing renumbers around it. It is also already documented, which is the distinction this corpus is built to draw: reserved-and-written-down is not the same as surface nobody asked for.

questions.against: You have one other behaviour in this corpus (BEH-LANG-1) making the same bet on the same deferred roadmap, and answering both the same way is how a v1 quietly acquires a v2's shape. `Word = 0` is the C# default for any enum whether or not a second member exists, so the renumbering argument protects against a hazard that only appears once someone adds a value — at which point they can append it. And a reserved member is not free in the way it looks: it is a branch every future `switch` has to handle or deliberately ignore, on a code path nothing can currently reach.

questions.title: Selection is deterministic for a given seed
contracts: the same seed picks the same word, so the sampler is testable
questions.asks: SelectNextAsync takes a required `int seed` and NOTHING calls it outside the tests — the drill API is PR 4 and does not exist. So where the seed comes from in production has never been decided, and it is a user-visible choice, not an implementation detail. Which is it: the client sends a seed, or the server makes one?

options.label: The server generates it per request
options.consequence: The drill route makes a fresh seed each call. Determinism reverts to what DESIGN.md:66-67 says it is for — unit-testability — and every draw is independent. A refresh gives a different card. Resuming a session mid-way is then a separate feature with its own state, not something the seed gives you.

options.label: The client supplies it per session
options.consequence: The frontend mints a seed when a drill starts and sends it with each draw. The same session replays the same sequence, so a refresh or a reconnect resumes where it was rather than reshuffling. It also makes the sequence reproducible from a bug report. Cost: the seed is now part of the public API contract, and a client that reuses one gets the same word forever.

recommend.label: The server generates it per request
recommend.why: DESIGN.md:66-67 says the determinism exists so the sampler is unit-testable, and that is a claim about the test suite, not a promise to a user. A4 says the picker samples weakness-weighted from the active pool — that is a property of the WEIGHTS, and it holds either way, so the seed is buying nothing the design asks for. Keeping it server-side also keeps the failure mode small: a client that mishandles a seed can pin itself to one word, and that bug is invisible until someone notices they keep seeing 好.

questions.against: You are deciding this now, in a corpus, for a route that will be written in PR 4 — and the version that is harder to add later is the one being rejected. Making the seed part of the request from day one costs one optional query parameter and no state; retrofitting it means changing a shipped drill endpoint and regenerating the client. Resume-after-refresh on a phone is also not an exotic want for a drill app, and the pinned-to-one-word failure is preventable by advancing the seed per draw rather than by hiding it. There is a third answer this question does not offer: derive the seed from something stable you already have — user plus date — which gives a reproducible day without either a client contract or a decision about session state.

steps.text: activating checkbox:Ran also sets checkbox:Exercised to done for the same day without the user separately activating it — the brief's own words are "Exercised - auto ticked by running"; a generated test can see Ran's own badge appear but cannot see a DIFFERENT noun's state change as a consequence of this one, so the causal half of the rule is recorded here rather than smuggled into a given fixture no reviewer would read as a rule
